question: Why does the production side of theatre interest you more than acting or performing?
lookingFor: A genuine pull toward the craft of making shows happen, not a fallback story from a failed acting ambition.

bullets: Name the specific moment or role that showed you what production work involves
Explain what you enjoy about it that performing doesn't give you
Avoid framing it as a consolation prize for not being an actor
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I acted a little in school but what actually hooked me was the one week I stage managed our sixth form play, calling cues and watching the whole thing lock into place from the wings. I realised I love holding the whole picture together rather than being one part of it, the problem solving of making a scene change happen in eleven seconds in the dark. That feeling of the show only working because of decisions nobody in the audience ever sees is what pulls me toward production.

commonMistakes: Saying they wanted to act but weren't good enough
Giving a vague answer like 'I just love theatre' with no production-specific reason
Not distinguishing production from performing at all
followUps: What's a production role you haven't tried yet but want to?

question: Why do you want to study Theatre Production here rather than another course or just working your way up in a theatre?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons for this course tied to a genuine gap the applicant wants filled.

bullets: Reference a specific feature of the course, such as its in-house venue, industry placements, or particular strand like lighting or stage management
Explain what structured study gives them that working alone in a venue wouldn't yet
Connect it to a concrete goal or gap in their current skills
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've done backstage work at my local theatre but it's all been learned on the fly, and I know I'm missing the technical grounding, especially in lighting design and production management, that a structured course would give me properly. Your course stood out because students run a full public season in the in-house theatre from second year, which means I'd be making real decisions with real consequences rather than just shadowing. I want that combination of taught technical skill and genuine responsibility before I go into the industry.

commonMistakes: Praising the university in general terms that could apply anywhere
Arguing that formal study is unnecessary for theatre
Not naming anything specific about the course structure
followUps: What's missing from your current experience that this course would fill?

question: When did you first realise you wanted to work behind the scenes in theatre?
lookingFor: A specific, credible memory that shows genuine early engagement rather than a rehearsed origin myth.

bullets: Describe one concrete moment or production, not a vague lifelong love
Explain what specifically caught their attention about the backstage side
Show how that early spark led to further action, not just a nice memory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was thirteen and helping paint scenery for my school's production of Bugsy Malone, and I remember standing at the back during the dress rehearsal watching the flat I'd painted actually look like a street under the lights. Nobody in the audience would ever know I'd done it and that anonymity felt exciting rather than disappointing. After that I started turning up to every get-in I could find an excuse to help with, which is really how I ended up here.

commonMistakes: A generic 'I've always loved theatre since I was little' with no specific memory
Describing only watching shows, never working on one
The story not connecting to any follow-through
followUps: What did you do next after that experience?

question: Talk us through a production you've worked on. What was your role and what did you actually do?
lookingFor: Concrete, specific detail about real responsibilities, showing understanding of process rather than a vague credit.

bullets: Name the production, the venue or context, and the specific role held
Describe actual tasks and at least one decision or problem they handled
Reflect honestly on what they learned or would do differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was assistant stage manager on our youth theatre's production of Our Town, which meant running props and calling the scene changes from the prompt corner during the run. The trickiest bit was a costume change we'd only allowed forty seconds for, so I ended up redesigning the backstage layout so the actor's next costume was pre-staged on a rail right by her exit point. It taught me that most stage management problems are really just logistics problems if you look at them early enough, and I'd build in that kind of buffer from day one next time rather than discovering the issue in tech week.

commonMistakes: Naming a show but not actually describing what they did
Taking credit for the whole production rather than their specific role
No reflection or learning, just a list of tasks
followUps: What would you change if you did that production again?

question: Tell us about a production you've seen where the production design or staging really stayed with you. What made it work?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuinely watching theatre with a production eye, able to name specific technical or design choices.

bullets: Name a specific production and what element of the production, not the acting, stood out
Explain the technical or design choice in enough detail to show real observation
Connect it to how it affected the audience's experience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a touring production of An Inspector Calls and the set, the house on stilts that literally collapses partway through, completely changed how I watch design now. What stayed with me was how the sound cues and the lighting state shifted together right before the fall, so your body tensed up before you consciously understood why. It made me realise good production design isn't decoration around the story, it's actually doing narrative work the script alone can't do.

commonMistakes: Talking only about the plot or the acting performance
Being too vague to prove they actually saw the show closely
Naming something they clearly haven't seen live or in detail
followUps: Have you seen anything that used design badly, and what went wrong?

question: In your own words, what does a stage manager actually do?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate grasp that the stage manager runs the show and coordinates the whole team, not just prompts lines.

bullets: Distinguish rehearsal-room duties from running the live show
Mention calling cues and being the central point of communication for the whole crew
Note the responsibility for safety and keeping the show consistent night to night
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In rehearsals the stage manager tracks blocking, props and any changes so the whole production stays consistent, and once the show opens they're the person calling every lighting, sound and set cue over headset so everything happens in the right order. They're really the hub the whole backstage team reports through, and they're responsible for the show running safely and the same way every single night. It's less about prompting actors and much more about holding the entire technical machine together in real time.

commonMistakes: Reducing the role to just feeding actors forgotten lines
Confusing stage manager with director
Missing the live cue-calling responsibility entirely
followUps: How is that different from a production manager's job?

question: What's the difference between a stage manager and a production manager?
lookingFor: Clear separation of the two roles by scope and timeframe, showing real understanding of how a production team is structured.

bullets: Explain the production manager oversees budget, scheduling and departments across the whole build
Explain the stage manager focuses on the room, then the running of the live show
Show awareness that the two roles work closely together but at different altitudes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The production manager is really running the whole production from above, sorting the budget, the build schedule and making sure the set, lighting, sound and costume departments are all hitting their deadlines and talking to each other. The stage manager is more embedded day to day, first running the rehearsal room and then calling the actual show once it's up. So the production manager's job is mostly done by the time the show opens, while the stage manager's job is only just starting properly at that point.

commonMistakes: Using the two titles interchangeably
Only describing one role and guessing at the other
Missing that the production manager's focus shifts before opening while the stage manager's peaks
followUps: Which of those two roles appeals more to you, and why?

question: What does 'blocking' mean in a rehearsal context?
lookingFor: Correct, confident use of a basic term with a sense of why it matters practically, not just a dictionary definition.

bullets: Define blocking as the planned movement and positioning of actors on stage
Note that it's usually set by the director and recorded by the stage manager
Mention why consistency matters, for cues, sightlines and safety
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Blocking is the specific movement and positioning the director sets for each actor at each moment, where they enter, where they stand for a line, when they cross the stage. It gets recorded in detail, usually by the stage manager in the prompt book, because everything else, the lighting cues, the sound timing, the sightlines from different seats, gets built around exactly where people are standing. If blocking drifts night to night it can throw off cues or even become a safety issue if someone ends up somewhere a set piece is about to move.

commonMistakes: Confusing blocking with line delivery or characterisation
Not mentioning who records it or why consistency matters
Giving an answer too vague to show real rehearsal-room experience
followUps: Who's usually responsible for recording blocking, and how?

question: What actually happens during a technical rehearsal, and why is a cue-to-cue different from a full run?
lookingFor: Understanding of the practical purpose of tech, distinguishing it correctly from dress rehearsals and full runs.

bullets: Explain tech is where lighting, sound, set and cues get set and rehearsed against the actors
Describe cue-to-cue as jumping between cue points rather than playing every scene in full
Note why this saves time when cues, not performance, are the priority
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Tech is where all the technical elements, lighting states, sound cues, set moves, actually get layered onto the show for the first time with the actors, rather than rehearsed separately. A cue-to-cue means you skip straight to a few lines before each cue, run the cue, check it looks and sounds right, then jump to the next one, rather than performing every scene in full. It's much faster because in tech week the priority is making sure two hundred cues fire correctly and safely, not polishing performances, which is what the later dress rehearsals are for.

commonMistakes: Treating tech rehearsal as just another full run of the show
Not knowing what cue-to-cue means at all
Confusing tech rehearsal with dress rehearsal
followUps: What would you do if tech was running badly behind schedule?

question: You notice a piece of set has a sharp edge that wasn't in the original design, and the show opens tomorrow. What do you do?
lookingFor: Prioritising safety over schedule, with a sensible, proportionate process rather than panic or ignoring it.

bullets: Flag it immediately to the relevant person, such as the production or stage manager
Propose a practical short-term fix, like padding or taping, alongside a proper long-term fix
Show they wouldn't let a deadline pressure them into ignoring a safety issue
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd flag it straight away to the production manager rather than deciding myself whether it's fine, because safety calls shouldn't be made alone under time pressure. In the short term I'd suggest something like edging tape or foam to make it safe for tomorrow's show, and separately push for it to be properly sanded or capped before the run continues past opening night. I'd rather delay a scene change slightly to fix it than let a preventable injury happen just because we were close to curtain.

commonMistakes: Deciding to ignore it because the show opens tomorrow
Fixing it alone without telling anyone in charge
No concrete short-term safety measure offered
followUps: What would you do if you were overruled and told to leave it as is?

question: Your set design has been cut in half by the budget two weeks before rehearsals start. How would you handle it?
lookingFor: Resourceful, collaborative problem-solving that protects the storytelling rather than just complaining or giving up quality.

bullets: Reprioritise which elements actually serve the story most and cut from there
Look for cheaper alternatives such as reused materials, hire, or simplified builds
Communicate proactively with the director and team rather than making silent cuts
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd do is sit down with the director and work out which elements of the design are actually doing storytelling work and which are just nice to have, because a budget cut is really a prioritisation exercise. I'd look hard at what we could hire, borrow, or repaint from a previous production's stock instead of building fresh, since that's usually where the real savings are without losing impact. And I'd tell the whole team early rather than quietly scaling things back, because a scenic painter or props maker working toward a budget they don't know has changed just wastes everyone's time.

commonMistakes: Treating the cut as purely a design problem to solve alone
Refusing to compromise on the original vision at all
Not mentioning communication with the rest of the team
followUps: What would you cut first, and what would you protect no matter what?

question: What would you do if you strongly disagreed with a director's staging or design choice, but it was ultimately their call?
lookingFor: Understanding of the production hierarchy and how to advocate professionally without either staying silent or overstepping.

bullets: Recognise the director has final creative authority
Raise the concern clearly and once, backed by a practical or safety reason if there is one
Commit fully to executing the decision once it's made, rather than sabotaging it quietly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd raise it once, clearly, and ideally framed around a practical concern, whether it's achievable in the time or budget we have, rather than just saying I don't like it, because taste alone isn't my call to make. If the director hears me out and still wants to go ahead, I'd commit to making it work as well as it possibly can, because a half-hearted execution helps nobody and undermines the whole show. I've learned that being useful in this job means having opinions but knowing whose decision it actually is.

commonMistakes: Refusing to accept the director's authority at all
Staying completely silent even when they have a genuine practical concern
Suggesting they'd quietly do it their own way instead
followUps: Has that ever actually happened to you? What did you do?

subtopic: Handling a live show going wrong
question: A piece of set fails to move during a live performance. What do you do in that moment?
lookingFor: Calm, practical improvisation that prioritises audience and cast safety and keeping the show running.

bullets: Stay calm and assess quickly whether it's safe to continue or needs an immediate stop
Communicate fast and clearly with the crew and cast over headset or established signals
Have a fallback in mind, such as improvised staging or a hold, rather than freezing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: First I'd quickly judge whether it's actually unsafe or just not ideal, because those need very different responses. If it's safe to carry on, I'd get on headset immediately and let the actors and crew know so they can adapt around it rather than everyone discovering it separately mid-scene. If it genuinely can't continue safely, I'd rather call a brief hold and fix it than let the show limp through something dangerous, because the audience will forgive a pause far more than an accident.

commonMistakes: Freezing or panicking instead of making a quick decision
Not mentioning communicating with the rest of the team
Treating every technical failure the same regardless of safety risk
followUps: How would you debrief the team after the show that night?

question: Tell us about a time you disagreed with someone else on a production crew. How did you resolve it?
lookingFor: A real, specific example of professional conflict resolution within a production team context.

bullets: Describe a genuine disagreement specific to production work, not a vague generic conflict
Show how they listened to the other person's constraints or reasoning
Land on a resolution that served the show, not just their own preference
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During a get-in the lighting designer and I disagreed over where a boom stand needed to go, because it was blocking a wing exit I needed clear for a quick change. Instead of just insisting, I walked her through the timing of the change so she could see why the space mattered, and she showed me why that angle was the only one that avoided a shadow on a key moment. We ended up shifting the change point five seconds earlier in the scene instead, which solved both problems without either of us losing what we needed.

commonMistakes: Picking a conflict unrelated to actual production work
Framing themselves as simply right and the other person as wrong
No real resolution or compromise described
followUps: What would you have done if you couldn't find a compromise?

question: Can you explain the difference between a proscenium arch stage, a thrust stage, and theatre in the round?
lookingFor: Accurate, confident grasp of basic venue configurations and a sense of how each affects production choices.

bullets: Define each configuration by where the audience sits relative to the stage
Note at least one practical production consequence of each, such as sightlines or set design
Avoid mixing up which is which
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A proscenium arch is the classic picture-frame stage where the audience sits facing one direction, which gives you the most control over what they can and can't see. A thrust stage juts out with audience on three sides, so you lose that one clean sightline and design has to work in the round on at least part of the set. Theatre in the round has the audience surrounding the whole stage, which is the hardest to design for because there's genuinely no backstage hiding spot and every piece of scenery has to look right from every angle.

commonMistakes: Mixing up thrust and in the round
Only defining the terms with no production implications
Describing them purely in terms of audience experience, not staging challenges
followUps: Which configuration would you find hardest to design a set for, and why?

question: What do you think a lighting designer needs to consider beyond just making sure the actors can be seen?
lookingFor: Understanding that lighting shapes mood, focus and storytelling, not just visibility.

bullets: Mention mood, time of day, and emotional tone as functions of lighting
Note directing audience focus to specific parts of the stage
Show awareness of practical constraints like rig time, budget, and the venue's equipment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Visibility is really just the baseline, after that a lighting designer is shaping mood, telling the audience where to look, and signalling things like time passing or a shift in tone without a word being said. A cold blue wash and a warm amber state can make the exact same set feel like two completely different places. Beyond the creative side there's also the practical reality of how many hours you actually have to rig and focus, and how many instruments the venue even owns, which shapes what's realistically possible.

commonMistakes: Reducing lighting design to purely functional visibility
Ignoring practical constraints like rig time or budget
Giving a purely technical answer with no mention of storytelling
followUps: Have you ever worked with lighting yourself? What did you learn?

question: How would you approach designing a set for a small venue with a limited budget and no fly system?
lookingFor: Practical, creative thinking about working within real constraints rather than an unconstrained dream design.

bullets: Prioritise flexibility, such as modular or multi-purpose pieces, over elaborate single-use scenery
Consider what can be achieved through suggestion and lighting rather than literal building
Show awareness that no fly system means scene changes must happen at stage level
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Without a fly system I'd think in terms of pieces that can be repositioned or reconfigured by hand quickly, rather than big single-purpose set walls that need to disappear upward. I'd lean on a few strong, flexible elements, maybe a rostrum and some flats that can represent multiple locations with small changes, and let lighting do a lot of the work suggesting a shift in place rather than rebuilding it from scratch each scene. Constraints like that usually push you toward more inventive, theatrical solutions than an unlimited budget would anyway.

commonMistakes: Designing as if the constraints didn't exist
Not addressing how scene changes would physically happen without flying
Treating budget limits as purely a negative with no creative response
followUps: Can you think of a real production that solved a similar constraint well?

question: What does a sound designer actually contribute to a production?
lookingFor: Understanding that sound covers reinforcement, effects, and atmosphere, and works closely with the wider design.

bullets: Mention both practical elements like microphones or reinforcement and creative elements like effects and underscore
Note that sound helps build atmosphere and can signal time, place, or emotion
Show awareness that sound design has to be timed precisely with cues, like other departments
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A sound designer handles the practical side, making sure voices and any music are actually heard properly in the space, but they're also building atmosphere with effects and underscore that can completely change how a scene lands emotionally. A single rumble of thunder or a distant door slam can tell the audience something about the world before anyone says a word. All of that has to be timed as precisely as a lighting cue, which is why sound is really its own full design discipline rather than an afterthought.

commonMistakes: Reducing sound design to just playing background music
Ignoring the reinforcement and technical side entirely
Not connecting sound to storytelling or atmosphere
followUps: Can you think of a moment where sound design really shaped how a scene felt?

question: Why does a costume department need to be involved early in the production process, not just before the show opens?
lookingFor: Understanding that costume affects movement, quick changes, and other departments, so needs early integration.

bullets: Mention that costume affects blocking and movement, so actors need to rehearse in approximations early
Note quick changes need to be planned and timed well before tech week
Show awareness that costume choices interact with lighting and set colours
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If costume only turns up right before opening, actors are suddenly moving in long skirts or heavy coats they've never rehearsed in, and blocking that worked in trackies can genuinely fall apart. Quick changes especially need planning way in advance, because a costume that looks great but takes ninety seconds to get out of is a real problem if the next entrance is in twenty. There's also a design conversation that needs to happen early, since costume colours can clash badly or vanish completely under certain lighting states if nobody's checked in advance.

commonMistakes: Treating costume as purely cosmetic with no functional impact
Not mentioning quick changes or movement
Assuming costume only matters visually, not for lighting or set coordination
followUps: How would you handle a costume that turns out to be impossible for a quick change?

question: What is a 'get-in', and why does the order things happen in matter so much?
lookingFor: Understanding of the practical logistics of loading a set into a venue and why sequencing is a real skill.

bullets: Define get-in as bringing the set, lighting rig, and other elements into the venue and building it
Explain that some tasks physically depend on others being finished first
Note the time pressure, since venues are often only available for a fixed window
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A get-in is the process of physically bringing the set, the lighting rig, sound equipment and everything else into the venue and building it all from an empty space. The order really matters because you genuinely can't focus lights properly until the set is built and in its final position, and you can't safely rig lighting above a stage that still has scaffolding on it from set construction. Venues usually only give you the space for a fixed number of days, so a badly sequenced get-in can eat the time you actually needed for technical rehearsal.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the term at all
Describing get-in as just moving in furniture with no sense of sequencing
Missing the time pressure element
followUps: How would you plan a get-in schedule if you only had two days?

question: Is there a theatre company or production team whose work you admire? What do they do that stands out to you?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with current theatre practice beyond just naming a famous show.

bullets: Name a specific company or production team, not just a play title
Explain a specific production choice or approach that stands out, ideally technical or design-related
Show ongoing engagement, not a single fact recalled for the interview
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I really admire Punchdrunk for how they build entire physical worlds the audience actually walks through, rather than watching from a fixed seat, because it means every prop and every corner of a room has to hold up to close inspection. What stands out to me is how much of that is production work rather than performance, the sheer amount of detailed set dressing and environmental design needed to make a warehouse feel like a genuine hotel from the 1930s. I've read a bit about how their design teams work months ahead of the performers on world-building, which is the kind of production-led process I'd love to be part of.

commonMistakes: Naming a famous actor or playwright instead of a production-focused answer
Vague praise with no specific detail
Clearly reciting something memorised with no real understanding
followUps: What would you want to learn from working with a company like that?

question: What extra production challenges do immersive or promenade productions create compared to a traditional seated show?
lookingFor: Sophisticated understanding of how audience movement changes lighting, sound, safety, and stage management.

bullets: Mention that lighting and sound have to work from many angles rather than one fixed audience direction
Note the safety and crowd management challenges of an audience that moves freely
Address the difficulty of cueing and stage management when performers and audience share unpredictable space
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: With a promenade show you lose the one fixed audience angle everything else gets designed around, so lighting and sound have to work convincingly from multiple directions since you genuinely don't know where everyone's standing. Safety becomes a much bigger production job too, because you're managing a moving crowd around performers and set pieces rather than a seated audience that stays put. Stage management gets harder as well, since cues often can't be tied to a fixed script moment in the usual way when performers might be improvising slightly to accommodate where the audience actually is.

commonMistakes: Only discussing it from an audience experience angle, not production
Not mentioning safety or crowd management at all
Assuming it's simply harder with no specific reasoning why
followUps: How would you approach lighting a scene with audience on every side of it?

question: What do you think theatre production has learned from the rise of streamed and hybrid live performances?
lookingFor: Balanced, informed view on how digital formats have changed production practice, not just an opinion on whether it's good.

bullets: Mention specific production adaptations, such as camera-aware lighting or multi-angle sound design
Acknowledge both the access benefits and the ways it differs from live production
Avoid simply declaring streamed theatre is not real theatre without engaging with the production side
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it forced production teams to design for two audiences at once, the people in the room and a camera that sees the stage completely differently to the human eye, so lighting states that read fine live can look flat or blown out on screen. It also opened theatre up to people who couldn't get to a venue for cost, distance, or access reasons, which I think is a genuine gain worth taking seriously rather than dismissing. I don't think it replaces being in the room, but it's pushed production teams to think harder about who a show is actually reaching.

commonMistakes: Dismissing streamed theatre outright with no production-specific reasoning
Only discussing it from an audience or artistic perspective, ignoring production adaptation
Showing no awareness that this is even a live industry conversation
followUps: Would you want to work on a hybrid production yourself? Why or why not?

question: What could a production team do to make a show more accessible, beyond just offering a captioned or audio-described performance?
lookingFor: Thoughtful understanding that access is a production-wide consideration, not a single bolt-on performance.

bullets: Mention considerations like relaxed performances, sensory adjustments, or backstage crew training
Show awareness that access affects design choices, such as strobe warnings or sound levels, not just special showings
Avoid treating access as a box-ticking exercise separate from the main production process
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Beyond the specific captioned or audio-described nights, I think access has to be baked into the design conversation from the start, things like flagging strobe or loud sudden sound cues clearly, or offering a relaxed performance where the house lights stay slightly up and the audience can move freely. It also means training front-of-house and backstage staff properly so access isn't just a policy on paper but something the whole team actually understands on the night. I think the mistake is treating access as one extra performance bolted onto the run rather than a lens the whole production process should go through.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning captioning or audio description with nothing further
Treating access purely as a marketing or box office issue
No specific production examples, just vague good intentions
followUps: Have you seen a production handle this particularly well or badly?

question: Where do you see yourself in this industry after you graduate, and how does this course get you there?
lookingFor: A grounded, informed sense of direction connected specifically to what the course can build.

bullets: Give a plausible direction, such as a specific department or type of venue, without over-specifying an exact job title
Connect that goal to specific skills or opportunities the course offers
Show awareness that early career in theatre production often means varied, entry-level work across venues
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd like to end up in production management, ideally at a regional producing house where you get to see a show through from first read-through to closing night, because I like that whole arc rather than just one slice of it. I know the early years will probably mean varied work across smaller venues and touring shows before that's realistic, and I think that's exactly the right way in. Your course's placement year with a producing theatre is the specific reason I think it gets me there faster than trying to learn everything on the job alone.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically specific plan with no room for the industry's actual entry points
A goal with no connection to the course at all
Sounding uncertain whether they even want a career in this field
followUps: What's the first job you'd realistically expect to take after graduating?
